title: Reparameterisation & the log-var trick
blurb: Moving randomness outside so gradients can flow

hook.title: Roll a standard die, then stretch it
hook.text: Imagine training a machine that *rolls a dice* in the middle and a result at the end. You'd like to know how nudging the machine's dials changes the final score, but the dice-shaking is a black box: you can't differentiate through randomness. The trick: **roll a fixed standard die first** ($\epsilon$, from $\mathcal N(0,1)$, outside the machine), then use the dials to stretch and shift the roll: $z=\mu+\sigma\epsilon$. Now the randomness is just an input and the dials ($\mu,\sigma$) sit in an ordinary differentiable formula.
hook.recall: Remember the standard die: sample $\epsilon$ outside, then $z=\mu+\sigma\epsilon$ is a deterministic, differentiable function of $\mu,\sigma$. The network can output $\log\sigma^2$ so any real number is a valid output.

explore.intro: Grey: the standard normal die $\epsilon$. Green: its stretched, shifted version $z$. Toy objective $r(z)=(z-2)^2$.
tasks: Move $\mu$ and $\log\sigma^2$: the green histogram is just the grey one stretched and shifted.
Compare the reparameterised gradient estimates with the true ones. Increase $K$.
explore.takeaway: $\nabla_\phi\mathbb E_{q}[r(z)]=\mathbb E_{\epsilon}[\nabla_\phi r(g(\epsilon;\phi))]$ with $g=\mu+\sigma\epsilon$; estimate by Monte Carlo and backprop. The log-var trick: $z=\mu+e^{\log(\sigma^2)/2}\epsilon$.

questions.prompt: Why is the reparameterisation trick used?
options: To let gradients flow to $\phi$ through the sampled $z$ by writing $z=g(\epsilon;\phi)$ with the randomness outside
To avoid computing the KL term
To reduce the number of layers
questions.explanation: The gradient w.r.t. $\phi$ is the harder one because the expectation depends on $\phi$; moving the randomness out makes it differentiable.
$e^{\ln4/2}=e^{\ln2}=2$. Outputting the log lets the network use any real number while keeping $\sigma>0$.

questions.prompt: Which statement about reparameterisation is FALSE?
options: It makes $z$ a deterministic function of $(\epsilon,\phi)$
It estimates $\mathbb E_\epsilon[\nabla_\phi r(g(\epsilon;\phi))]$ with Monte Carlo
It works for any discrete latent variable
questions.explanation: The slide states it only works for continuous $z$ (and only some distributions). REINFORCE is the general alternative mentioned later.

questions.prompt: Which gradient is “easy” and which is harder for the ELBO?
options: $\nabla_\theta$ easy; $\nabla_\phi$ harder, since the expectation depends on $\phi$
questions.explanation: With $\theta$ the expectation’s distribution doesn’t change; with $\phi$ it does.

questions.prompt: *“I sample $z\sim\mathcal N(\mu,\sigma^2)$ and backpropagate through the sampling step: sampling is differentiable.”* The error:
options: Sampling itself isn’t differentiable w.r.t. its parameters; reparameterise: sample $\epsilon$ then set $z=\mu+\sigma\epsilon$
Backprop can’t be used with Gaussians
questions.explanation: Black-box dice vs standard die plus dials.
